# Question

**Does sleep deprivation hurt one's ability to interpret facial expressions?** Killgore, Balkin, Yarnell & Capaldi had 54 healthy adults recognize Ekman morphed faces after a rested night vs 23.5 h awake (within-subject).

## Data source

Reconstruction of per-participant percent-correct (20 trials per emotion) calibrated to means digitized from the paper's Fig. 3; paired-SD calibration documented.

# Exploratory analysis

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean recognition difference (deprived − rested) by emotion"
emotions = ["happiness", "sadness", "surprise", "fear", "disgust", "anger"]
diffs = [(df[f"{e}_deprived"] - df[f"{e}_rested"]).mean() for e in emotions]
sig = [e in ("happiness", "sadness") for e in emotions]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 4))
ax.bar(emotions, diffs,
       color=["#c76c6c" if s else "#999999" for s in sig])
ax.axhline(0, color="k", lw=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Mean difference (deprived − rested), % correct")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

# Methods & results

Paired t-tests per emotion, sign-flip randomization on paired differences (100k), and percentile bootstrap CIs; overall average also tested.

| Emotion | Mean diff (deprived − rested) | Randomization p |
|---|---|---|
| Happiness | −1.30 | **0.0050** |
| Sadness | −2.59 | **0.0047** |
| Surprise | −0.46 | 0.78 |
| Fear / disgust / anger | ≈ 0 | n.s. |
| Overall average | ≈ 0 | 0.86 |

# Decision

The deficit is **emotion-specific**: recognition of happiness and sadness is impaired while the average across emotions looks null (p = 0.86). Averaging would have masked the effect entirely — a nice argument against blindly collapsing multi-outcome experiments.
